fixes.explanation: They pleaded with Him, “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over.” (Luke 24:29) Pleaded is about as close to beg as you get. They didn't just say a polite goodbye. I think they weren't ready for that walk to end.

Luke says, “…their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.” (Luke 24:16) Jesus is right there beside them and they don't know it's Him. The text says their eyes were kept from it, and it doesn't tell us more than that. You know when someone waves at you at the gym and you have no idea who it is? Same problem, much bigger moment.

Cleopas asks, “Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in recent days?” (Luke 24:18) I think he's amazed that the stranger hasn't heard. I bet those days felt huge to the two of them.

They don't mention Galilee at all. They call Jesus of Nazareth “…a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people.” (Luke 24:19) Their description is about how powerful He was in speech and action, not about where He taught.

That's not how they describe Him. Cleopas and his friend say Jesus was powerful in speech and action “…before God and all the people.” (Luke 24:19) They say nothing about Him staying away from crowds.

They say, “Our chief priests and rulers delivered Him up to the sentence of death, and they crucified Him.” (Luke 24:20) That's how they tell it to the stranger. It's a heavy part of the story. I think the sadness on their faces fits.

Rebuild isn't their word. They say, “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” (Luke 24:21) Notice it's “we were hoping,” not “we are hoping.” I think that tells you their hope felt shaky by then.

Judge isn't their word. They say, “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” (Luke 24:21) Their hope is about redeeming Israel, not judging it. I think that “were” in “we were hoping” sounds like a hope with a shadow over it.
They really do say it. Cleopas and his friend tell the stranger, “…it is the third day since these things took place.” (Luke 24:21) The third day is part of what they lay out for Him.

The text says otherwise. Some of their companions went to the tomb and found it just as the women had described. Then comes the line, “But Him they did not see.” (Luke 24:24) They found the tomb as described, but they did not see Jesus.

That's right. The companions found the tomb just as the women had described, and the two say, “But Him they did not see.” (Luke 24:24) So the tomb matched the women's story, but the companions did not see Jesus. These two are still carrying a lot of questions on that road.

Jesus asks, “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26) Suffer is the first blank. He puts it as a question: was it not necessary? He's pointing them to what the Christ was to go through.

Luke says, “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.” (Luke 24:27) Moses and all the Prophets are where Jesus begins. From there, He explains what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself. I'd pay a month of cookie money to have heard that walk.

The text names a different starting point. Jesus began “…with Moses and all the Prophets…” and then explained what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself (Luke 24:27). The Psalms aren't named in this verse. Moses and all the Prophets are where Luke says He began.

They ask each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32) They say it after they recognize Him. Looking back, they could tell something was happening inside them all along. I think that's a good feeling to look back on.
